title: Culture—or a much bigger story?

elements.text: We started with a question. Six countries made the answer more complicated.
Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8, 9–16); McSweeney (2002, pp. 93–107). National averages are not individual traits or causal scores. Full references: p. 27.

Not one Africa.
Not one Asia.
Ghana and South Korea give us a striking comparison. Botswana, Mauritius, Malaysia and the Philippines challenge the easy explanations.
We think culture matters. But different histories, resources and starting points make “Africa versus Asia” the wrong shortcut.

sources: Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8, 9–16); McSweeney (2002, pp. 93–107). National averages are not individual traits or causal scores. Full references: p. 27.

title: Same empire. Different inheritance.

elements.text: Ask what colonial rule built, extracted and left behind—not just which flag it flew.
These studies do not show that colonial rule was beneficial overall, or that one empire explains the six countries’ later paths.
Bolt et al. (2025, pp. 1–6, 18–20); Huillery (2009, pp. 176–180, 203–208); Kohli (1994, pp. 1277–1284); Haggard et al. (1997, pp. 867–881); Dolan (1993), archival passage recheck pending.
British African councils varied. Investment also varied within French West Africa. An empire label hides important differences (Bolt et al., 2025; Huillery, 2009).
Researchers disagree about Korea’s colonial inheritance. Organisation mattered, but so did coercion, unequal ownership, division, war and later policy change (Kohli, 1994; Haggard et al., 1997).
The Philippines combined formal institutions and education with concentrated power. Spanish and US rule cannot be explained by a British–French contrast (Dolan, 1993; recheck pending).
Independence did not reset the economy. We think what countries inherited—and what they could build on afterwards—mattered more than the colonial flag alone.

sources: Bolt et al. (2025, pp. 1–6, 18–20); Huillery (2009, pp. 176–180, 203–208); Kohli (1994, pp. 1277–1284); Haggard et al. (1997, pp. 867–881); Dolan (1993), archival passage recheck pending.
limit: These studies do not show that colonial rule was beneficial overall, or that one empire explains the six countries’ later paths.

title: Track is not the whole story.

elements.text: Track is not the whole story.
Ghana: the useful question is who the railway connected.
One railway case cannot explain all of Africa or show that infrastructure alone caused growth. It does not establish the net benefit of colonial rule.
Jedwab and Moradi (2012, pp. 1–4, 6–10). Original schematic based on cited facts, not traced map geometry. Full reference: p. 27.

Solid: original connections to mines and Kumasi.
Dashed: later economic links—not a mapped railway route.

Built to extract.
Used for more.
Lower transport costs also supported cocoa production and urban growth. Original purpose and later effects were not the same (Jedwab & Moradi, 2012).

title: Six countries. Six starting points.

elements.text: What could each country build on—and what held it back?
These are contemporary photographs, not scenes from independence. They give context, not proof of historical living conditions or causes.

Cocoa exports; inherited roads, rail and Tema harbour.
Few inherited public assets and limited skills; mineral income later changed the base.
Sugar dominated export earnings; diversification came later.
Colonial inheritance was disrupted by division and war.
Commodity exports came before export manufacturing; federation formed in 1963.
Formal institutions and education coexisted with concentrated power.

title: Build. Learn. Improve. Repeat.

elements.text: A country needs more than factories. People and firms need the ability to make better things.
This is a possible learning sequence, not an automatic cycle. Institutions, resources, distribution and access to technology and markets shape every link.
Education helps people use and improve technology.
Reliable power and transport help work get done.
Local businesses need links, skills and organisations.
Production tests quality, routines and coordination.
Export markets can bring scale and feedback.
Use returns to upgrade—not just protect failure.
The chain breaks when power fails, feedback is ignored, or firms are protected from learning.

limit: This is a possible learning sequence, not an automatic cycle. Institutions, resources, distribution and access to technology and markets shape every link.

title: “Made here” is not the whole story.

elements.text: “Made here” is not the whole story.
A country can export a product without keeping all its value—or learning how to make its most complex parts.
Export totals and photographs cannot reveal who keeps the value, how much is local, or which skills firms have learned.

World Bank (2020, Box 2, pp. 44–47); Nasution (2000, pp. 19–20, Table 9); World Bank (1993, pp. 20–26). Conceptual journey, not measured product shares. Photographs: jgmorard (2009), Port Klang; george ruiz (2013), Metro Manila; CC BY 2.0. Full credits p. 29.

Port Klang, Malaysia · 2009
Containers show movement—not local value kept.

Metro Manila, Philippines · 2013
Market exchange—not a national productivity measure.
Local work is one part of the value.
Local links may deepen—or stay thin.
Manufacturing share measures production mix, not technological capability. More assembly does not automatically mean deeper domestic learning.

title: Not an overnight miracle.

elements.text: South Korea built skills and firms over time. It also made costly policy mistakes.
The sequence cannot isolate culture as the cause. Other countries cannot copy its history, security setting or international opportunities.
World Bank (1993, pp. 20–26, 127–130, 159–161, 242). Rodrik (1995): competing investment-coordination argument; registered working-paper abstract, not a page-specific causal estimate.
Education, agricultural change and infrastructure helped build foundations.
Credit and investment worked alongside export incentives and performance pressure.
Heavy industry expanded, but brought debt, bottlenecks and other costs.
Policy adjustment accompanied deeper firm learning and technological upgrading.
Learn from South Korea. Don’t photocopy it. We value cooperation and long-term effort, but these are lessons to adapt—not proof of a superior culture.

sources: World Bank (1993, pp. 20–26, 127–130, 159–161, 242). Rodrik (1995): competing investment-coordination argument; registered working-paper abstract, not a page-specific causal estimate.

title: A lens. Not a national personality.

elements.text: A lens. Not a national personality.
Hofstede’s six dimensions ask about patterns in societies—not what every person is like.
National averages are historical, country-level lenses—not individual personalities, timeless truths or causal scores. Missing country scores are not invented.
Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8, 9–16); McSweeney (2002, pp. 93–107). National averages are not individual traits or causal scores. Full references: p. 27.
How strongly are people tied to groups? Not a trust score.
Competition and achievement versus care and quality of life. Historical labels.
How do people respond to ambiguity? Not simply risk-taking.
Future-focused adaptation versus present and past obligations. Not policy duration.
How strongly does society regulate gratification? Not work ethic.
Culture matters. It isn’t destiny. We think habits and shared expectations influence cooperation—but history, resources and institutions also shape what people can do.

sources: Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8, 9–16); McSweeney (2002, pp. 93–107). National averages are not individual traits or causal scores. Full references: p. 27.

title: Trust whom—with what?

elements.text: Trust in a relative, a bank and “most people” are not the same thing.
Governance indicators are not trust measures. Different questions, years and survey samples cannot be turned into one six-country trust ranking.
OECD (2017, pp. 41–44, 62–79); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8, 12). No comparable six-country direct-trust series is available for this comparison. Full references: p. 27.

Accra market, Ghana · 2020
Amuzujoe; CC BY-SA 4.0. Everyday trade—not a trust score. Full credit p. 29.
Someone you know is different from a stranger.
Family and close contacts can support cooperation.
Name it: a court, a bank or a government.
Wording, timing and who was asked all matter.

We cannot conclude that
“Asia trusts more”.
That was our initial impression—not a finding supported by comparable evidence across these six countries.

title: Family first. Doors open—or closed?

elements.text: Close ties can make cooperation easier. They can also make it harder for outsiders to join.
This is a conditional explanation and a discussion prompt—not a measure of any country’s culture, corruption or trust.
OECD (2017, pp. 41–44, 62–79); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8, 12). No comparable six-country direct-trust series is available for this comparison. Full references: p. 27.

Gyeongdong Market, Seoul · 2008
Gaël Chardon; CC BY-SA 2.0. Market context, not measured trust. Full credit p. 29.
Credit, labour and mutual help can keep people and businesses going.
Hiring outsiders or sharing control may be harder without reliable organisations and contracts.
Who would you trust with money?
Family? A friend? A bank? An unfamiliar partner backed by a reliable contract?
We see family networks mainly as a strength. But conflict, exclusion and closed-minded decisions can turn that strength into a limit.

sources: OECD (2017, pp. 41–44, 62–79); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8, 12). No comparable six-country direct-trust series is available for this comparison. Full references: p. 27.

title: Strong leadership. Honest feedback.

elements.text: Planning ahead helps only if people can challenge mistakes.
Cultural scores cannot replace direct evidence about decisions, investment, policy duration or whether leaders actually correct failure.
Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8, 9–16); McSweeney (2002, pp. 93–107). National averages are not individual traits or causal scores. Full references: p. 27.
Hierarchy may coordinate action—or silence the people who notice a problem.
Long-term plans need feedback. A long-term-orientation score does not measure policy continuity.
NOT ENOUGH EVIDENCE FOR A GROWTH CLAIM

Uncertainty avoidance: need observed behaviour and matched timing.
Masculinity / femininity: need a clear mechanism and valid measures.
Indulgence / restraint: need a direct, timed link—not guessed work ethic.
Strong government—for whose benefit? We support long-term planning, but leaders must serve the country, face accountability and change policies that fail.

sources: Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8, 9–16); McSweeney (2002, pp. 93–107). National averages are not individual traits or causal scores. Full references: p. 27.

These are our hypotheses—not established laws or national scores.

Ask how it works.
Look for the case that breaks it.
What would change our minds? Better measurements, a clear sequence in time, and evidence against competing explanations.

title: More roads—or better connections?

elements.text: What if the important difference is whom infrastructure connects?
Connections alone do not guarantee diversification. Skills, investment, resources, institutions and market access remain competing explanations.

Maipose (2008, pp. 3–5, 8–11); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8); World Bank (2020, Box 2, pp. 44–47); Nasution (2000, pp. 19–20). Full references: p. 27. World Bank (1993, pp. 20–26). Original group hypothesis.

Perai Industrial Zone, Malaysia · 2024
HundenvonPenang; CC BY-SA 4.0. Industrial context, not proof of linkages. Full credit p. 29.
South Korea, Malaysia and Mauritius fit a story of skills, firms, infrastructure and markets working together.
Botswana grew despite few inherited public assets. The Philippines shows that export access can coexist with thin domestic links.

Roads matter when people
and firms can use them.
Revise the claim if stronger connections followed growth rather than helped produce it.

sources: Maipose (2008, pp. 3–5, 8–11); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8); World Bank (2020, Box 2, pp. 44–47); Nasution (2000, pp. 19–20). Full references: p. 27. World Bank (1993, pp. 20–26). Original group hypothesis.

title: Can cooperation reach strangers?

elements.text: AFRICA & ASIA / TEST 2 / RADIUS OF TRUST
Contracts, courts and organisations may let people work together without knowing each other first.
We cannot show that generalized trust caused larger firms or national growth. Institutional substitutes and other causes remain unresolved.

OECD (2017, pp. 41–44, 62–79); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8, 12). No comparable six-country direct-trust series is available for this comparison. Full references: p. 27. Original group hypothesis.
Reliable institutions may help cooperation extend beyond family and close contacts.
We lack comparable direct-trust evidence across all six cases. Ghana and South Korea remain direct-trust gaps.

Trust matters to us.
The regional claim is unproven.
Reopen with comparable, weighted trust surveys linked in time to firm outcomes, while testing institutional alternatives.

sources: OECD (2017, pp. 41–44, 62–79); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8, 12). No comparable six-country direct-trust series is available for this comparison. Full references: p. 27. Original group hypothesis.
limit: We cannot show that generalized trust caused larger firms or national growth. Institutional substitutes and other causes remain unresolved.

title: Keep the direction. Fix the mistakes.

elements.text: Keep the direction. Fix the mistakes.
A stable policy is useful only if it can learn.
Policy duration cannot be separated here from state capacity, resources, foreign investment, market access, shocks or prior success.

Maipose (2008, pp. 3–5, 8–11); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8); World Bank (2020, Box 2, pp. 44–47); Nasution (2000, pp. 19–20). Full references: p. 27. World Bank (1993, pp. 127–130, 159–161, 242). Original group hypothesis.
Give firms and workers a direction.
South Korea, Mauritius, Malaysia and the Philippines are consistent with durable direction plus correction.
Continuity can preserve failure. Botswana warns that accumulating wealth is not the same as diversifying production.
Revise if lasting policy repeatedly protects failure rather than learning.

sources: Maipose (2008, pp. 3–5, 8–11); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8); World Bank (2020, Box 2, pp. 44–47); Nasution (2000, pp. 19–20). Full references: p. 27. World Bank (1993, pp. 127–130, 159–161, 242). Original group hypothesis.
limit: Policy duration cannot be separated here from state capacity, resources, foreign investment, market access, shocks or prior success.

title: The cases that break the shortcut.

elements.text: The cases that break the shortcut.
Four countries stop us telling one simple continental story.
No case proves a universal formula. An exception challenges a claim; it does not automatically prove a rival explanation.

Maipose (2008, pp. 3–5, 8–11); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8); World Bank (2020, Box 2, pp. 44–47); Nasution (2000, pp. 19–20). Full references: p. 27. Photos: Paul tk (2018), Mochudi; Richard N Horne (2025), Port Louis. Full credits p. 29.
Supports resource management and investment. Challenges the need for strong inherited infrastructure. Does not prove broad diversification.

Mochudi solar pumping · 2018
Infrastructure context, not a growth estimate.
Supports adaptation and diversification. Challenges fixed cultural destiny. Does not prove continuity alone caused growth.

Port Louis sugar terminal · 2025
Trade context, not a history series.
Malaysia: exports can help, but do not prove local capability.
Philippines: global links alone are not enough. There is no single “Asia” path.
Mauritius surprised us. Its small size challenged our assumptions about what a country needs to develop—and about one single African development story.

title: Build the ability to do more.

elements.text: Build the ability to do more.
Skills. Reliable connections. Firms that learn. Institutions that make cooperation possible.
This is a bounded interpretation, not a calculation of each cause’s contribution. Six countries do not represent two whole continents.
Group synthesis: World Bank (1993, pp. 4–7, 20–26, 79–80); World Bank (2020); Maipose (2008); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014); Hofstede (2011).

Divergence depended less on fixed regional culture than on whether states, firms, workers and external partners built and disciplined productive capabilities over time. Education, agricultural change, infrastructure, investment coordination, technology access and exports mattered in different sequences. Their effects depended on institutions, resources, distribution, history and international conditions. Culture may influence coordination, legitimacy and organisational practice, but it is not a stand-alone explanation.

sources: Group synthesis: World Bank (1993, pp. 4–7, 20–26, 79–80); World Bank (2020); Maipose (2008); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014); Hofstede (2011).
limit: This is a bounded interpretation, not a calculation of each cause’s contribution. Six countries do not represent two whole continents.

title: A bigger economy. A better life?

elements.text: A bigger economy. A better life?
For us, development is about what people can actually do and afford—not just a bigger GDP number.

Group values and interpretation, not a measured six-country wellbeing comparison. GDP charts: World Bank (2026), NY.GDP.PCAP.KD. Policy implications: World Bank (1993, 2020); Maipose (2008); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014); OECD (2017).

Health.
Buying power.
Freedom.
Living standards.
Higher income matters. But we also care about what that income buys, whether people are healthy, and whether they have more freedom. GDP alone cannot answer those questions.
Build skills and useful connections. Keep a direction, but correct failure. Help people cooperate beyond close ties. Adapt each lesson to the place.

sources: Group values and interpretation, not a measured six-country wellbeing comparison. GDP charts: World Bank (2026), NY.GDP.PCAP.KD. Policy implications: World Bank (1993, 2020); Maipose (2008); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014); OECD (2017).

title:
Different starts.
No fixed destiny.

elements.text: Culture matters—but the question is bigger than culture.
Group viewpoint informed by the six-country comparison. On cultural change: Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8, 16); Beugelsdijk and Welzel (2018, pp. 1469–1475, Figures 7–9).
We think “Why couldn’t Africa grow like Asia?” is misleading. Neither continent followed one path. Countries had different histories, resources, infrastructure and opportunities.
We still think culture can shape trust and cooperation. But the evidence pushes us to ask what governments, firms and people could build—and what helped or blocked them.

If culture matters,
can culture change?

sources: Group viewpoint informed by the six-country comparison. On cultural change: Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8, 16); Beugelsdijk and Welzel (2018, pp. 1469–1475, Figures 7–9).
